newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grain - Japan starting February soy buying.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Japan starting February soy buying.

text.p: Japan will begin gradually buying U.S. soybeans this week for February 1997 shipment while Taiwan and the Philippines may pick up U.S. wheat, East Asian traders said on Monday.

"We're gradually buying U.S. soybeans for February shipment," a soybean trader in Tokyo said. "But basically we'd like to get a clear picture of vegetable oil demand during the April-June period next year before launching active buying."
Japanese premiums for U.S. soybeans are currently quoted at 120 U.S. cents a bushel over the Chicago Board of Trade's (CBOT) March contract.
But the Japanese corn market is seen remaining quiet until the end of this year, traders said.
"Buying U.S. corn for January-March shipment is over," a corn trader said. "Some feed makers may buy for April-June shipment, but most will adopt a wait-and-see stance."
Japanese feed makers expect further price drops in the world corn market by early next year, traders said.
Premiums for U.S. corn were quoted at 98 to 100 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT's March 1997 contract against 97 to 98 cents a week earlier.
Traders added that Japanese feed makers are expected to increase corn buying from Argentina for April-June 1997 shipment in an attempt to trim their dependence on U.S. corn.
In Taiwan, the Taiwan Flour Mills Association is likely to tender for up to 72,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat, while corn and soybean buyers will sit out of the market, traders said.

Flour Mills Association official Lu Wei-chih said in Taipei that one shipment of 34,000 tonnes in the tender should be delivered from December 15 while a second shipment of 38,000 tonnes would be for delivery from December 30.
Philippine flour companies may also re-enter the market if wheat prices continue sliding this week, Manila traders said.

The December CBOT wheat contract closed 4-1/2 U.S. cents down on Friday at $3.96 a bushel. In Minneapolis, where the Philippines buys most of its wheat, the March contract finished 5-1/2 cents down at $3.81-1/2 a bushel.
In South Korea, a delegation from Canada was expected to spark local buyers' interest in feed grains this week.
"There seems to be some negotiations between the Canadian delegation and Seoul buyers for feed grains, especially feedwheat and feed barley," said a trader with a Seoul-based Japanese trading house.

The delegation, including representatives from the Canadian Wheat Board, Canada Grain Commission, and Candian International Grain Institute visited South Korean feed milling companies from last Friday and held a seminar on Monday to promote its feed grain exports to South Korea, said an official with the Canadian embassy in Seoul.
South Korean feed processors are still expected to buy Canadian feedwheat to cover their needs for February and March shipment, traders said.
"I believe that our clients are still looking for Canadian feedwheat though they have delayed the purchase several weeks," said the Japanese trader.
"But it is difficult to match deals since they are looking for the feedwheat (at) just below US$130 a tonne C&F," he said. said. Feedwheat is being traded at around $140 a tonne C&F.
In the corn market, he said "most buyers will wait until January since they have covered their needs for May to June shipments."
Trade sources said they expected the Korea Feed Association would pass on tenders for at least 50,000 tonnes of feedwheat this week due to higher than expected prices.
The sources said arrival of the wheat was set for January 30 at Inchon and Ulsan.

A trader with the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation said the freight premium to South Korean ports from the Pacific Northwest was slightly down to $13 a tonne from $14 last week, and the freight premium from the U.S. Gulf was $23 a tonne from $24 a week ago.
